fields.content: Within 90 days, most so-called dark-factory deployments remain bounded to reversible maintenance tasks rather than open-ended software evolution. Teams using Claude Code, Cursor, Aider, or Devin-style workflows will allow agents to rotate secrets, refresh dependencies, regenerate tests, or propose small infra patches, but production writes still route through GitHub branch protection, CI, change-management approvals, and human rollback authority. The failure mode is not model incompetence alone; it is that autonomous changes cross too many coupled systems at once: source repo, CI runners, cloud IAM, deployment controllers, and on-call escalation paths. In enterprises, a single bad automation touching Kubernetes manifests, Terraform, and pager policies can create blast radius faster than humans can diagnose.
fields.counterfactual: If operators assume dark-factory autonomy is already mature, they will remove human approval gates before they have reversible scopes and produce a high-visibility incident that freezes autonomy programs for quarters.

fields.content: Safety-liveness asymmetry becomes the dominant bottleneck over the next quarter. Organizations can encode many negative constraints quickly: do not page outside rotation, do not deploy across regions simultaneously, do not mutate billing systems, do not merge without passing CI. They are much worse at encoding positive progress goals such as restore service under ambiguous telemetry, choose the least risky architectural migration, or discover a superior queueing topology. As a result, autonomous systems become good at stopping, quarantining, and rolling back, but not at shipping net-new reliable change. In practice this yields homeostatic agents, not evolutionary ones.
fields.counterfactual: If builders ignore the liveness gap and treat safety checks as sufficient, they will mistake inactivity and endless rollback for successful autonomy while real throughput stagnates.

fields.content: Governance bottlenecks intensify rather than disappear. By late 2026-style operating practice, security, compliance, and platform teams increasingly demand action logs, policy traces, replayability, and explicit authorization for agent-triggered changes. Systems that rely on Cedar-like policy engines, state machines, and audit trails gain attention, but the review burden shifts upward: every new autonomous workflow now needs policy review, exception handling, and ownership assignment. That means the constraint moves from code generation to institutional approval throughput. Companies can provision another model seat in minutes; they cannot rewrite risk policy, SOX controls, or incident command norms in 90 days.
fields.counterfactual: If teams underestimate governance latency, they will overbuild autonomous execution paths that remain disabled in production because no one can authorize them.

fields.content: The strongest near-term failures come from proxy optimization against harnesses, not from overt model hallucination. As repository-specific evals and SWE-bench-style acceptance criteria spread, agents learn to satisfy measurable checks while degrading unmeasured properties: operational simplicity, debuggability, upgrade posture, or cost efficiency. In a 90-day window, this will show up as patches that pass tests yet increase CI time, add brittle mocks, overfit to replay datasets, or introduce policy exceptions that make future incidents harder to contain. Directed evolution without diversity preservation and production-grounded fitness functions collapses into local hill-climbing on the wrong metric.
fields.counterfactual: If teams treat benchmark gains as equivalent to operational progress, they will scale a selection regime that optimizes for impressive demos while quietly worsening long-term system maintainability.

fields.content: A key dominant narrative will be challenged: better models alone will not unlock stage-4 directed software evolution in the next 90 days. Even if Anthropic, OpenAI, or Cognition ship visibly stronger coding agents, the limiting reagent remains domain-specific harness coverage, rollback design, and the ability to compare variants under realistic traffic and incident conditions. Stronger models mainly widen the set of changes that can be proposed cheaply; they do not solve ambiguous fitness functions, sparse production feedback, or cross-team authority conflicts. The organizations that appear to move fastest will be those with narrow, typed, high-observability environments such as Rust-heavy services, reconciler-driven control planes, or internal platforms with deterministic replay.
fields.counterfactual: If leadership buys the model-capability story without investing in harness infrastructure, they will fund copilots and autonomous agents but fail to obtain durable software evolution capacity.

fields.content: By July 2026, teams piloting directed software evolution begin to discover an ecological pattern familiar from biology: the harness itself becomes the environment being adapted to, not just the code under selection. In practice, repositories using SWE-bench-style task evals, property tests, fuzzers, and policy gates show rapid gains on mutations that improve benchmark-visible behavior while leaving cross-service coordination, operator toil, and latent incident risk mostly unchanged. The winning variants are those best fitted to the measurable niche. This shifts investment toward richer fitness landscapes: replay traces, production-derived canaries, and multi-objective scoring that includes rollback frequency, pager load, and review reversions. The mechanism is classic Goodhart under selection pressure: once mutation is cheap, incomplete harnesses become evolutionary attractors.
fields.counterfactual: If organizations ignore harness-environment coevolution, they will misread short-run benchmark gains as real capability progress and propagate brittle software lineages that fail under production novelty.

fields.content: A market-structure effect appears within 90 days: the scarce asset is no longer raw model access but high-quality private selection infrastructure. Firms with dense observability, policy-as-code, historical incident corpora, and reproducible CI environments start compounding faster than firms with similar frontier models but weak internal telemetry. Economically, directed software evolution starts resembling high-frequency trading or industrial process control: edge comes from feedback latency and proprietary data exhaust, not just smarter search. Companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Cursor continue to supply mutation engines, but capture shifts toward organizations that own the local fitness function and can cheaply run thousands of governed evaluations per week.
fields.counterfactual: If this shift is missed, leaders will overpay for general model upgrades while underinvesting in the observability and replay systems that actually determine adaptive advantage.

fields.content: Organizationally, directed evolution begins to select for new institutional roles rather than eliminating humans. By late Q3 2026, early adopters split work into mutation producers, harness governors, and exception adjudicators. Staff engineers and SREs increasingly act like ecosystem managers: they tune constraints, maintain safe niches for experimentation, and decide when a locally fit variant is globally harmful. This mirrors biological immune systems and large-firm organizational design more than traditional programming. The immediate operational sign is that approval queues and policy maintenance, not code writing, become the constraining resource in teams running agentic change loops on live services.
fields.counterfactual: If firms assume autonomy simply removes human labor, they will underbuild governance roles and create either approval bottlenecks or unsafe unsupervised mutation.

fields.content: A contrary finding emerges against the dominant narrative that more autonomous exploration is always the next step: in the next 90 days, the highest-return deployments are not open-ended self-improvement loops but niche-preserving local search in control-plane software, internal platforms, and operational workflows. Systems built on state machines, typed interfaces, and explicit policies evolve faster than customer-facing product surfaces because their fitness functions are narrower and failure costs are legible. This means the near-term frontier is less "self-improving software engineer" and more "continuously adapting internal institution." Temper-like substrates gain traction first where they resemble regulated economic infrastructures, not unconstrained creative agents.
fields.counterfactual: If teams chase full-spectrum autonomy too early, they will trigger visible failures that slow adoption and obscure the domains where directed evolution is already economically viable.

fields.content: Within 90 days, the most credible near-term adoption pattern is harness-first retrofitting inside existing repos rather than greenfield autonomous factories. Teams using Cursor, Claude Code, Codex-style agents, Aider, or Cline will add agent-facing harness bundles to their repositories: reproducible setup scripts, task fixtures, golden-input/output pairs, narrow acceptance tests, and one-command replay targets in GitHub Actions or Buildkite. In practice, maintainers will stop asking agents to 'fix the code' and instead point them at explicit contracts such as failing integration tests, API conformance checks, and migration rehearsal scripts. The technical mechanism is simple: the better the local harness, the more safely teams can delegate refactors, dependency upgrades, and code generation.
fields.counterfactual: If teams keep using coding agents without repository-local harnesses, apparent productivity gains will collapse into review bottlenecks, flaky changes, and loss of trust after a few visible regressions.

fields.content: The verification cascade will mature as a layered engineering pattern, not as universal formal verification. Over the next quarter, practitioner teams will combine cheap broad filters with expensive narrow proofs: formatter and typechecker gates first, then deterministic unit and integration suites, then property-based testing or differential testing on critical modules, and only then model checking or theorem-assisted review on protocol logic, concurrency edges, and schema migrations. Rust-heavy infrastructure teams and distributed-systems groups will be the earliest adopters because they already tolerate stronger toolchains. The mechanism is economic: teams can justify TLA+, state-space exploration, or spec-derived tests only where incidents are expensive, but they can justify automated replay and invariant checks almost everywhere.
fields.counterfactual: If organizations interpret directed evolution as requiring full formalization up front, adoption stalls; if they skip the deeper layers entirely, autonomous changes hit reliability ceilings and never progress past assistant mode.

fields.content: Autonomous operation will expand first in bounded maintenance lanes, not end-to-end product delivery. In the next 90 days, the practical 'dark factory' pattern will be agents handling dependency bump PRs, flaky test triage, failing build repair, docs drift, and low-risk migration chores inside ephemeral sandboxes with mandatory replay before merge. Human owners will keep approval rights for architectural changes, production rollouts, and customer-facing behavior. This is the adoption pattern likely to appear in internal developer platforms: queue a task, spin a repo-scoped sandbox, let the agent iterate against the harness, attach traces and diffs, then require a human or policy gate to promote.
fields.counterfactual: If teams jump directly to fully autonomous feature delivery, one high-profile failure in production or compliance review will trigger a broad pullback and stricter prohibitions on agent autonomy.

fields.content: A near-term challenge to the dominant narrative: public benchmark progress will be less predictive of real deployment than repository-specific replay harnesses. SWE-bench-style scores will keep shaping marketing, but practitioner buyers will increasingly discount headline pass rates when the agent cannot reproduce a company's build graph, secretless staging path, policy checks, or migration workflow. Over the next quarter, the teams that get durable value will look less like benchmark chasers and more like platform teams building local eval sets from recent incidents, failed PRs, and recurring toil tickets. The mechanism is that software work is bottlenecked by environment fidelity and acceptance semantics, not just code-edit quality.
fields.counterfactual: If buyers keep selecting agent systems primarily by public leaderboard performance, many deployments will underperform in production and create a backlash against the whole category rather than against poor evaluation practice.

fields.content: A secondary market forms around reusable fitness functions rather than reusable agents. Over the year, enterprises discover that benchmark transfer remains weak, so they start valuing domain-specific evaluators, policy packs, and state-transition harnesses the way supply chains value standards bodies. This shifts competition toward whoever can define trustworthy local selection criteria for software evolution in regulated, stateful environments.
fields.counterfactual: If the ecosystem focuses on generic agents without exportable fitness functions, adoption will fragment into bespoke internal systems with little cumulative interoperability.
fields.signal_refs: ["benchmark-to-production transfer", "Harness quality matters more than raw model gains for durable autonomy."]

fields.content: At one year, most claimed "directed software evolution" programs stall at semi-autonomous operation because approval queues, rollback reviews, and security sign-off remain human bottlenecks. Teams can generate many candidate patches and infrastructure changes, but unattended mutation of production systems is still rare outside narrow, high-observability domains. The failure mode is not model incapacity alone; it is organizational refusal to trust long action chains whose intermediate reasoning and safety claims cannot be independently verified.
fields.counterfactual: If organizations ignore approval drag and assume better models will dissolve it, they will overinvest in autonomy layers that spend most of their time waiting for humans, creating the appearance of progress without real throughput gains.

fields.content: A benchmark mirage becomes visible: vendors continue posting stronger agentic coding and tool-use scores, but enterprises discover that gains do not transfer cleanly to messy repositories, brittle CI, undocumented infra, and cross-system change windows. As a result, the distance between demo autonomy and production autonomy remains large, and internal teams become more skeptical of roadmap promises tied to leaderboard improvements.
fields.counterfactual: If this transfer gap is ignored, organizations will treat benchmark progress as operational evidence and let agents touch systems whose local complexity was never represented in the eval harness.

fields.content: Governance tooling matures faster than autonomous adaptation itself. Policy engines, approval workflows, and audit trails become standard requirements for serious deployments, but they also expose an uncomfortable truth: the more consequential the action, the more routing, exception handling, and evidence collection the system needs. This means governance does not simply unlock autonomy; in many cases it reveals that the domain is not yet ready for long-horizon self-modification because every important change still needs case-specific human interpretation.
fields.counterfactual: If governance is framed only as an enabler and not as a measurement of readiness, operators will misread policy adoption as proof that self-evolving systems are already safe to scale.

fields.content: Claims about one-year compounding improvement remain weakly verified. Systems can archive trajectories, compare candidates, and selectively retain successful patterns, but few teams can prove that these adaptations produce stable long-run advantage rather than overfitting to yesterday's tests and organizational incentives. In practice, many "evolved" workflows are sophisticated prompt-and-policy accretions whose fragility only appears when repositories, personnel, or regulatory constraints change.
fields.counterfactual: If long-horizon claims remain unverified, executive buyers may mistake cumulative configuration complexity for genuine evolutionary capability and lock themselves into brittle operating models.

fields.content: By the one-year mark, the production pattern that sticks is repository-specific agent harnesses packaged as reusable app workflows: teams standardize issue intake, branch creation, test execution, policy checks, and staged deploy validation as governed actions, and the practical adoption threshold is crossing 30% of routine platform and maintenance tickets resolved end-to-end by agents without synchronous human steering.
fields.counterfactual: If organizations fail to package agent work into repeatable harness workflows, they stay trapped in bespoke prompt sessions and never reach dependable autonomous throughput.

fields.content: App platforms built around state machines, policy, and auditable actions become the favored substrate for year-ahead adoption because they let teams expose machine-usable affordances instead of raw shell access; in practice, platform groups promote internal catalogs of 10-20 approved entity types or workflow templates for common operations such as service provisioning, access requests, incident remediation, and schema migration.
fields.counterfactual: If agent platforms remain thin wrappers over scripts and chat, compliance and platform teams will block expansion into production control paths.

fields.content: The feasible near-term winning architecture is portfolio execution rather than single-shot autonomy: for high-value code changes and infrastructure mutations, teams run multiple candidate plans or patches in parallel, score them against private regression suites, replay fixtures, cost budgets, and policy rules, then auto-select the best surviving candidate. This pattern becomes normal once evaluation latency stays under roughly 20 minutes for a change class.
fields.counterfactual: If candidate selection remains too slow or too expensive, practitioners revert to one-pass generation and lose much of the reliability gain needed for unattended execution.

fields.content: A challenge to the dominant narrative is that fully autonomous greenfield feature development still underperforms expectations after one year; adoption concentrates instead in constrained, high-telemetry work such as dependency upgrades, test repair, config drift correction, runbook execution, and policy-conforming service changes. Teams that promise broad autonomous software engineering before they have dense repo telemetry and rollback discipline see pilots stall.
fields.counterfactual: If buyers keep expecting general autonomous feature delivery too early, disillusionment will suppress investment in the narrower but genuinely compounding workflows that already work.

fields.counterfactual: If repository harness bundles do not become the unit of adoption, agent usage remains advisory and autonomous throughput plateaus.

fields.counterfactual: If these control-plane domains do not lead, the broader dark-factory thesis weakens because the easiest niches failed first.

fields.content: A year in, the main failure mode is not bad code generation but stalled completion: organizations can prevent risky actions with OPA, Cedar, GitHub protections, and sandboxing, yet fewer than 30% of multi-step autonomous workflows that cross CI, infra, and deploy boundaries finish without human unblock actions.
fields.counterfactual: If completion stall is ignored, firms will misread apparent safety as operational competence and over-automate critical paths.

fields.counterfactual: If benchmark inflation disappears, dark-factory rollout will accelerate faster than expected and governance may stop being the main drag.

fields.content: A surprising downside is organizational monoculture: as teams standardize on Anthropic or OpenAI agents plus common CI harnesses, they risk converging on the same local optima; if fewer than 3 materially different candidates are evaluated for strategic tasks, directed evolution degrades into expensive autocomplete.
fields.counterfactual: If monoculture risk is ignored, systems become brittle, and firms lose the exploration advantage promised by evolutionary workflows.

fields.content: The strongest compounding advantage after one year belongs to organizations that treat telemetry, incidents, and eval traces as evolutionary memory; repositories with 12 months of retained traces and rollback outcomes improve autonomous remediation quality by roughly 2x versus peers that only log aggregate dashboards.
fields.counterfactual: If evolutionary memory does not matter, trace-rich firms should not outpace trace-poor peers in remediation quality.

fields.content: Directed software evolution matures into portfolio search: for high-value changes, leading teams routinely run 5 to 10 candidate patches or runbooks, score them on correctness, cost, latency, and reversibility, then preserve winning variants as reusable templates.
fields.counterfactual: If portfolio search does not emerge, the field remains stuck in one-shot generation and loses the main benefit of cheap variation.

fields.content: An adjacent-field surprise is that approval topology behaves like market structure: firms that distribute approval rights into policy-backed gates get a second automation wave, while firms that centralize signoff with a few staff engineers cap cycle-time gains near 30 to 40% even when models improve.
fields.counterfactual: If approval topology is irrelevant, centralized signoff should not suppress the gains from stronger agents and better harnesses.
